checkpoints: `reclaimPolicy: Delete` was the root cause of Incident 1 — it makes the CSI driver call `DeleteVolume`, deleting both the PV and the real data immediately when the PVC is deleted, with no confirmation step or safety delay, so an accidental `kubectl delete pvc` is unrecoverable.

Switching to `reclaimPolicy: Retain` fixes Incident 1 — when the PVC is deleted the PV only moves to phase `Released` and data stays on the real disk; an admin must actively patch the PV's `claimRef` to null before it can be reused or deleted, creating a safety net.

`volumeBindingMode: Immediate` was the root cause of Incident 2 — it provisions the PV the moment the PVC is created, before the scheduler has decided which node/zone the Pod will land on, so on a 3-zone cluster the provisioner can pick a zone with no suitable node, leaving the Pod permanently `Pending` since volumes can't attach cross-zone.

Switching to `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` fixes Incident 2 — provisioning is delayed until the first Pod referencing the PVC is already bound to a specific node, so the provisioner knows exactly which zone is needed and creates the PV there.

Adding `allowVolumeExpansion: true` is a sensible improvement that doesn't directly fix either incident — it lets the PVC capacity be grown online (editing `spec.resources.requests.storage`) when Postgres needs more disk, avoiding recreating the volume and migrating data.

Each of the three changed fields maps to exactly one incident (reclaimPolicy → Incident 1, volumeBindingMode → Incident 2), and the answer must state that mapping explicitly rather than just listing the new YAML, since the prompt asks which field solves which incident.

This StorageClass should be dedicated to the production database; ephemeral/test workloads that need fast deletion and don't care about zone should get a separate StorageClass (e.g. Delete/Immediate) rather than having this conservative config applied to every workload.
Decline the manager's suggestion — would not use the root account's access key for Terraform.
Root account = the email that registered the AWS account, holding absolute power such as changing billing, closing the account, or removing any security restriction.

Root's power cannot be restricted — no policy can ever be attached to root to limit it; because of this, AWS recommends enabling MFA on root, never creating an access key for it, and only using it for the handful of mandatory actions like billing changes or closing the account.
Everyday work — including Terraform calling the API — should go through IAM instead of root.

IAM is built from four blocks: user (a person/service identity), group (a bucket of users for centralized permission management), role (a temporary identity issuing short-lived credentials for services/cross-account access), and policy (a JSON document defining allowed/denied actions).
An identity's effective permission is the sum of every policy attached to it, directly or via a group.

Applying least-privilege here: create a dedicated IAM user (or role if running from CI/EC2) for Terraform, attaching only the policy it actually needs for the resources it manages, absolutely not AdministratorAccess.

Reasoning: if the IAM user's access key leaks, damage is bounded to the granted scope (can't touch billing or resources outside it), whereas leaking a root access key means losing the entire account with no way to revoke or bound the damage, since root simply doesn't accept a limiting policy.

Disagrees with determining it by name — a subnet name like `public-subnet-1a` is only a naming convention for humans with no technical meaning to AWS; what ACTUALLY decides whether a subnet is public or private is the route table associated with it.

A subnet is public when its route table has `0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway` PLUS the subnet attribute `map_public_ip_on_launch = true` — without that attribute, even with the correct route, the instance doesn't automatically get a public IP.
A subnet is private (egress) when its route table points `0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway` — allowing outbound traffic but not accepting direct inbound from the internet.
The data/isolated tier has no default route at all, reaching only internal VPC traffic — this is where RDS/ElastiCache go for maximum isolation.
Route tables use longest prefix match: a more specific route wins over a broader one, and a broad route wins over the default `0.0.0.0/0`.
Each subnet is associated with exactly one route table — without an explicit association it falls into the main route table.

A `/16` should be chosen for the VPC upfront because the VPC's primary CIDR cannot be resized after creation — you can only add a secondary CIDR via `associate-vpc-cidr-block`, never change the original block.
A `/16` gives enough IP space to slice subnets by AZ × tier (public/private/data) without running out of room as the system grows.

Identifies the root cause: a single NAT Gateway placed in us-east-1a is shared by the app instance in us-east-1b, forcing that instance's egress traffic to cross the AZ boundary before reaching the Internet Gateway.
Identifies the specific charge behind the spike: the cross-AZ data transfer fee ($0.01/GB), which is separate from and stacks on top of the NAT Gateway's existing processing fee ($0.045/GB).

Explains the cost impact: this fee stacking makes egress from the 1b instance cost noticeably more per GB than if the NAT Gateway sat in the same AZ — which is why the bill spiked even though total traffic stayed the same.

Explains the reliability risk: a NAT Gateway is only highly available within its own AZ (it doesn't replicate to other AZs), so an incident in us-east-1a would take down egress for both AZs, turning the multi-AZ design into a single point of failure at the NAT layer.
Proposes the fix: provision a separate NAT Gateway in EACH AZ (its own NAT GW for us-east-1a and its own for us-east-1b).

Specifies the route table redesign: each AZ's private subnet route table must point its 0.0.0.0/0 default route to the NAT Gateway in the SAME AZ, never crossing over to the NAT Gateway in another AZ.

States the outcome of the fix: it eliminates the cross-AZ egress charge entirely and removes the NAT-layer single point of failure, so one AZ going down no longer takes the whole system's internet access with it.
Suggests how to confirm the fix: compare the NAT Gateway line item in Cost Explorer before/after the route table change, or use VPC Flow Logs to verify traffic no longer crosses AZ boundaries.
Loại SG khỏi nghi vấn: SG là stateful (đã allow 443 inbound thì response cùng connection tự động được phép ở egress, không cần rule egress riêng) nên vấn đề không nằm ở SG.
NACL là stateless — không nhớ connection, nên mỗi chiều inbound và outbound cần rule riêng, độc lập với nhau.
Rule inbound của NACL đã đúng: mở port 443 để nhận HTTPS request từ client.
Rule outbound hiện tại chỉ mở mỗi port 443 — đây chính là chỗ sai (root cause của bug).
Khi server trả response, nó không gửi từ port 443 đến port 443 của client, mà source port là 443 còn destination port là ephemeral port do OS của client chọn ngẫu nhiên (thường trong dải 1024-65535).

Hệ quả: response gửi tới ephemeral port của client bị NACL REJECT ngay tại egress (vì outbound rule chỉ cho phép destination port 443) — client không nhận được reply nên bị timeout, dù server log cho thấy đã xử lý và gửi response.
Cách fix: thêm một `aws_network_acl_rule` egress mới với rule_action = "allow", from_port = 1024, to_port = 65535, protocol tcp, để mở đúng dải ephemeral port cho chiều outbound.

Cách verify sau khi fix: retest bằng `curl -v https://<server-ip>` từ bên ngoài để xác nhận có response trả về, hoặc dùng VPC Flow Logs lọc theo ACTION = REJECT trên ENI của server để xác nhận không còn record reject.

Points out that db-sg's ingress hardcodes CIDR blocks (10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.2.0/24) to work around auto-scaling app server IPs changing, instead of using SG-to-SG reference (referenced_security_group_id) to allow by security-group identity rather than static IP range.

Explains the concrete risk of the hardcoded CIDR approach: if the subnet later gains another AZ, or the auto-scaling group launches an instance outside exactly those listed CIDR ranges, the DB connection gets silently blocked — a bug that's hard to catch because the SG still looks correct, only surfacing when debugging a failed DB connection.

Points out the PR mixes two rule-management styles in the same codebase — app-sg declares ingress inline inside aws_security_group, while db-sg's egress is a separate aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule resource — making it harder to audit where a given SG's actual rules live.
Points out the newly added egress rule for db-sg opens ip_protocol = "-1" (every protocol) to 0.0.0.0/0, which a database has no reason to need and which violates least privilege.
Explains the security consequence: if the DB were compromised (e.g. SQL injection leading to RCE), this wide-open egress would let an attacker exfiltrate data anywhere on the Internet unimpeded.
Proposes changing db-sg's ingress from a hardcoded CIDR to referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.app.id.
Proposes making the whole PR consistent by using separate resource rules (aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule/egress_rule) throughout, with no inline ingress{}/egress{} left anywhere.

Proposes narrowing db-sg's egress to actual needs — e.g. if it only needs to reach Secrets Manager/KMS via an internal VPC endpoint, egress should open only port 443 to that endpoint's prefix list, not the entire Internet.
S3 and DynamoDB should use a Gateway Endpoint — the only endpoint type that supports these two services.

A Gateway Endpoint works by inserting a managed prefix-list route into the subnet's route table (no ENI), so matching traffic goes straight to the service instead of through the NAT Gateway or Internet Gateway.
SSM is not on the Gateway-endpoint-supported list, so it must use an Interface Endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink instead.
An Interface Endpoint works by creating an ENI with a private IP inside the subnet, attached to a security group that only needs port 443 open since all AWS APIs are HTTPS.

private_dns_enabled must be set to true so a private hosted zone is created and the canonical name ssm.<region>.amazonaws.com resolves to the endpoint ENI's private IP, meaning no code or SDK endpoint URL changes are needed.

Gateway Endpoints are entirely free (no hourly charge, no per-GB data processing charge); Interface Endpoints are not free (hourly charge per ENI/AZ plus per-GB) but are still much cheaper than routing that traffic through the NAT Gateway.

Once all three endpoints are in place (Gateway for S3/DynamoDB, Interface for SSM), NAT Gateway is no longer needed for this traffic, and if the fleet has no other internet-bound calls the NAT Gateway can be removed entirely to eliminate that cost line.
Validate the change using VPC Flow Logs to confirm traffic to S3/DynamoDB/SSM no longer passes through the NAT Gateway's ENI, and compare the NAT Gateway line in Cost Explorer before and after.

Ingress rule is written as a separate/standalone resource — `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule` — not an inline `ingress {}` block inside `aws_security_group.db`, satisfying the "separate resource rule" requirement (independently plannable/taggable/destroyable).
`security_group_id = aws_security_group.db.id` attaches the rule to the db security group, i.e. defines who is being granted access into db.
`referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.app.id` is used instead of `cidr_ipv4` — the SG-to-SG reference mechanism that allows by security-group identity rather than a fixed IP/CIDR range.

This SG-reference mechanism is what satisfies the "survive auto-scaling" requirement: membership is evaluated dynamically at connection time, so any instance currently carrying the `app` SG is allowed through regardless of its IP — newly launched/replaced instances are automatically covered with no manual rule update needed.
Port/protocol are scoped to the minimum necessary for Postgres: `from_port = 5432`, `to_port = 5432`, `ip_protocol = "tcp"` — not broadened to `-1` (all protocols) or a wider port range.
Overall verdict: disagree with sharing the S3 Gateway Endpoint across the 8 VPCs via Transit Gateway, but agree with sharing the SSM Interface Endpoint from the shared-services VPC.

A Gateway Endpoint (used for S3) is not an ENI — it is only a managed prefix-list route inserted into the route table of the exact VPC that contains it, so there is no IP address for other VPCs to route to via Transit Gateway or peering.

If the other 7 VPCs try calling S3 without their own Gateway Endpoint, their traffic simply doesn't match any prefix-list route, so depending on route table config it either falls through to a NAT Gateway/Internet or fails outright.

The correct solution for S3 is for each of the 8 VPCs to create its own Gateway Endpoint; since a Gateway Endpoint is entirely free, this is not a cost issue, just a few repeated lines of config (which a shared Terraform module can avoid copy-pasting).
An Interface Endpoint (used for SSM) is a real ENI with a specific private IP address in the shared-services VPC's subnet.

Because it has a real IP address, the other 7 VPCs' route tables CAN point to that IP via Transit Gateway, exactly the same way they'd route to any other internal resource in the shared-services VPC — so the proposal of one shared Interface Endpoint for SSM is reasonable and cost-effective.

Sharing the Interface Endpoint requires DNS resolution to work across VPCs: enable private_dns_enabled = true on the endpoint and configure Route 53 Resolver rules (or private hosted zone VPC association) so the other 7 VPCs resolve ssm.<region>.amazonaws.com to the shared endpoint's private IP — otherwise their SDKs would still call the public endpoint.
States that the "wait a few more minutes" advice is wrong because no background node-boot process exists — there is nothing that additional time would fix.

Explains that `status: ACTIVE` only reflects the AWS-managed control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler) being up and able to serve `kubectl` requests — it says nothing about whether any worker node exists.
States that on EKS the control plane and data plane are provisioned as fully separate, decoupled steps — creating/activating a cluster never automatically creates any EC2 worker node.
Identifies that getting an actual node requires explicitly declaring a data-plane resource: either a managed node group (`aws_eks_node_group`) or a Fargate profile.
Knows that a managed node group's EC2 instances are launched and lifecycle-managed via an AWS-managed Auto Scaling Group, not created manually.
Specifies that the node IAM role must trust the EC2 service principal (`ec2.amazonaws.com`) so instances can assume it.

Names all three managed policies required on that role: `AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy` (kubelet operation), `AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy` (VPC CNI IP assignment), and `AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly` (image pulls).

Recognizes the near-miss failure mode — an existing node group whose role is missing one policy produces a node that appears in `kubectl get nodes` but stays stuck `NotReady` (kubelet can't register / CNI can't assign IPs), distinct from the empty-list case — and concludes the fix is to check whether a node group/Fargate profile is declared at all and whether its IAM role has every required policy, rather than waiting.
